questions.prompt: Why do API testers sometimes check the database after a POST succeeds?
options: To confirm the data was actually stored correctly, not just echoed back in the response
Because API responses are never trustworthy
To make the test run faster
Because status codes are optional
questions.explanation: A 201 response can echo the request body even when persistence is wrong (truncated, mis-mapped or not committed). A targeted DB check confirms the stored state. Responses are usually trustworthy for what they claim; DB checks add speed cost, not speed.

questions.prompt: Which database account should an automated API test use for its verification queries?
options: A read-only account scoped to the test database
The production admin account
The application's own owner account with DDL rights
Any account; it does not matter in test
questions.explanation: Verification only needs SELECT. A read-only, test-scoped account limits damage if a query is wrong. Admin or owner accounts can alter schema or data by mistake, and production credentials never belong in tests.

questions.prompt: A database assertion should look up the exact row the test created (for example by the returned id) rather than counting all rows in the table.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Counting the whole table breaks as soon as other tests or users insert rows in parallel. Looking up by the id returned from the API checks exactly the record this test is responsible for.

questions.prompt: This check is flaky: it sometimes finds no row even though the API returned 201. What is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
resp = api.post('/orders', json=order)
assert resp.status_code == 201
row = db.fetchone('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = %s', [resp.json()['id']])
assert row is not None
options: The write is processed asynchronously (queue or eventual consistency), so the row may not exist yet when the query runs
SQL is case-sensitive on column names
The API returned the wrong status code
Parameterised queries are slower
questions.explanation: If the API accepts the request and persists through a background worker, an immediate SELECT can race the write. Poll with a timeout instead of a single query (or a fixed sleep). The status code was correct, and parameters do not cause missing rows.

questions.prompt: POST /customers returned 201. Which database checks add real value? Select all that apply.
options: Stored values match the request after any documented normalisation (e.g. trimmed email, lower-cased)
Server-generated fields such as created_at and status are set correctly
Sensitive fields such as the password are stored hashed, never in plain text
The table still has the same column names as yesterday
questions.explanation: Normalisation, server-set fields and hashing of secrets are invisible in most responses but matter. Re-checking the schema on every test is a migration or contract concern, not a per-request assertion.

questions.prompt: PATCH /orders/7 changes the status to cancelled and returns 200. The orders row shows cancelled, but the stock reservation rows for that order still exist. What should you report?
options: A defect: the cancel did not release related data, a side effect the API response could not show
Nothing, because the response and the order row agree
A test bug, because tests should only check the response
A performance issue
questions.explanation: Database validation is about the whole effect of the operation, including related tables. The response and main row look right, which is exactly why a DB check of side effects found the bug.

questions.prompt: This helper is meant to verify a customer by email. Which problem is the most serious?
questions.code:
def find_customer(email):
    return db.fetchone("SELECT id, email FROM customers WHERE email = '" + email + "'")
options: It builds SQL by string concatenation, so test data with a quote breaks it and it models an injection-prone pattern; use a parameterised query
It uses fetchone instead of fetchall
It should use SELECT * for completeness
Email columns cannot be queried
questions.explanation: String-built SQL fails on values like O'Brien and teaches an injection-prone habit. Parameters fix both. fetchone is fine when email is unique; SELECT * makes tests brittle to new columns.

questions.prompt: Your suite deletes every row in orders before each test so DB counts are predictable. Tests now pass alone but fail randomly in the parallel CI job. What is the best fix?
options: Give each test its own unique data (e.g. a run-id prefix) and assert on the specific rows it created, cleaning up only those
Run all tests serially forever
Add retries to the failing tests
Truncate the table more often
questions.explanation: Global truncation lets one test wipe another's data. Unique per-test data plus targeted assertions makes tests independent and parallel-safe. Serial runs and retries hide the problem rather than fix it.

coding.title: Verify the order a test created
coding.prompt:
Your API test created order `ord_102`. Write a query returning that order's `id`, `status` and `total` from `orders`.

Expected: one row `ord_102 | open | 59.5`.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE id = 'ord_102';
coding.explanation: Filtering by the exact id the API returned makes the check independent of any other rows in the table.
hints: Use a WHERE clause on the primary key.
SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE id = ...
coding.setup:
CREATE TABLE orders (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, status TEXT, total REAL);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('ord_101',1,'paid',20.0),('ord_102',2,'open',59.5),('ord_103',2,'cancelled',12.0);

coding.title: Find order items with no parent order
coding.prompt:
After a bulk API import, check referential integrity: list the `id` of every row in `order_items` whose `order_id` has no matching row in `orders`, ordered by `id`.

Expected ids: 4, 5.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT oi.id FROM order_items oi LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY oi.id;
coding.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every item; where no order matched, the order columns are NULL. Filtering on `o.id IS NULL` keeps exactly the orphans, including the item whose order_id is NULL (a NOT IN subquery would behave differently with NULLs).
hints: Start from order_items and LEFT JOIN orders.
Unmatched rows have NULL in the joined table's columns.
WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY oi.id

coding.title: Compare an API response with the stored row
coding.prompt:
Write `diff_record(api, row, mapping)` that compares an API response dict with a DB row dict. `mapping` maps API field names to DB column names. Return a sorted list of API field names whose values differ. Treat strings as equal if they match after stripping whitespace and ignoring case **only for the field `email`**.

Example: `diff_record({'name':'Ravi','email':'A@X.COM'}, {'full_name':'Ravi','email':'a@x.com'}, {'name':'full_name','email':'email'})` returns `[]`.
coding.explanation: Walking the mapping keeps API names and column names separate, which is exactly the problem in real systems (camelCase JSON, snake_case columns). Normalising only the documented field avoids hiding real defects elsewhere.
hints: Loop over `mapping.items()` to get (api field, db column) pairs.
Use `.get()` so a missing column counts as a difference.
Lower-case and strip both sides only when `field == 'email'`.

tests.name: Case is only ignored for email
Missing column counts as a difference
